text: Consider a primitive disk that has 50 tracks. A seek takes 5 ms (on average) to move the arm head per track. On an average, without optimization (to try to put sequential file data in blocks with close proximity) two logically consecutive blocks in a file will be about 10 tracks apart. however, with an optimization attempt to cluster related blocks, the mean inter-block distance can be reduced to 2 tracks. If the rotational latency is 50 ms and the transfer time is 15 ms per block, how long does it take to read a 50-block file in both cases.
answer: It takes 15 msec to transfer one block, thus transferring 50 blocks takes 750 msec. If the average number of tracks to move is 10, then at 5 msec per track this will take 2500 (5x10x50) msec for a 50 block file. Lastly, the rotational latency is 50 msec and is added for every block, thus total is 2500 msec rotational delay. Thus the non-optimized solution for this problem is 750 + 2,500 +  2500 = 5750 msec to transfer a 50 block file. Optimization only alters the mean interblock distance to 2 tracks and thus reduces seek time from 2500 to 500 (5x2x50) msec. Thus the total time for an optimized disk is (750 + 500 +2,500  =) 3750 msec.

text: Base register of segment 0
answer:
To calculate this, find a valid reference to segment 0. For example:
VA 0x00000005 (decimal: 5) --> VALID in SEG0: 0x00000205 (decimal: 517)
Here you can see that virtual address 5 translates to physical address 517. Subtracting the offset into segment 0 (5) from 517 gets us 512, which must be the base address (0x400 in hex).

text: Bounds register of segment 0
answer:
For this, you need to find (in the best case) two references, one that is at virtual address N and is valid, and one that is at address N+1 but is not valid; that will tell us the bound precisely. And hence:
VA 0x0000001d (decimal: 29) --> VALID in SEG0: 0x0000021d (decimal: 541)
VA 0x0000001e (decimal: 30) --> SEGMENTATION VIOLATION (SEG0)
This tells us that any virtual address from 0 through 29 is valid, whereas 30 is not. Hence, the size of segment zero is 30, which we thus conclude is the bound. If you want the physical address instead, it is base plus size, or 542.

text: Base register of segment 1
answer:
Similar to the question above, but remember that segment 1 goes backwards:
VA 0x0000006c (decimal: 108) --> VALID in SEG1: 0x000003ec (decimal: 1004)
Thus, if 108 maps to 1004, we know that 127 (the last valid byte of the virtual address space) would map to 1023 (add 19 to 108 gets us 127; thus add 19 to 1004 to get 1023). Hence, the base (as described in the notes) would be 1024, just beyond the end of where the backward-growing segment lies.

text: Bounds register of segment 1
answer:
The bound here is harder, because it is imprecise.
VA 0x00000050 (decimal: 80) --> SEGMENTATION VIOLATION (SEG1)
VA 0x00000058 (decimal: 88) --> VALID in SEG1: 0x000003d8 (decimal: 984)
As you can see, 80 goes too far backwards, but 88 is fine. With 88, the size must at least allow 88 through 127 to be valid; thus 40 bytes is the minimum segment size. It clearly could also be that 81 is valid, which adds 7 more bytes into the segment size, or 47. Thus, the size of this segment is between 40 and 47, inclusive

How does the valid bit in the TLB entry differ from the valid bit in the page table entry ? Explain.
answer: A TLB valid bit refers to whether a TLB entry has a valid translation within it. When a system boots, for example, a common initial state for each TLB entry is to be set to invalid, because no address translations are yet cached there. Once virtual memory is enabled, and once programs start running and accessing their virtual address spaces, the TLB is slowly populated, and thus valid entries soon fill the TLB. In a page table, when a page-table entry (PTE) is marked invalid, it means that the page has not been allocated by the process, and should not be accessed by a correctly-working program. The usual response when an invalid page is accessed is to trap the OS, which will respond by killing the process.

State the dynamics of wait( ) call and explain the reason behind involving mutex lock in this design. Also briefly state the need for using a while() loop for the predicate check in the calling of the wait() operation.
answer:
The wait() on CV, puts the caller to sleep + releases the lock (atomically), otherwise how could another thread acquire the lock and change the state and/or signal it to wake up? Also if putting to sleep + releases the lock both is not done atomically then also there is a race condition so that is also taken care by this call. Before returning after being woken up, wait() re-acquires the lock, thus ensuring that anytime the waiting thread is running between the lock acquired at the beginning of the wait sequence and the lock release at the end, it holds the lock. This design of wait() call thus is very convenient for application use so that programmer need not worry about concurrency issues coming up.
When a condition variable is signaled to wake up a thread, it is removed from the wait queue but before that thread reacquires the mutex, another thread may be given CPU time (and potentially the mutex). Therefore, the thread must do another check when it actually acquires the mutex to ensure the condition it needs to proceed is still true.

text: State 2 main benefits of multithreading? What are the possible sources of overhead associated with multithreading?

There are two main benefits of multithreading, namely parallelization and concurrency (on single CPU) i.e is the hiding of I/O latency.
Adding threads make sense if you have fewer threads than you have cores or if you are performing many I/O requests. Adding threads can lead to pure overhead otherwise.

text: Why is LRU considered a good page replacement policy? Describe a case where it performs badly.

text: How are reference bits used to implement an approximate LRU?
answer: Upon a memory reference to a page, algorithm assumes that the hardware will set a bit saying that the given page has been accessed. The OS, when it needs a page, will then sweep through the pages of memory in a circular (or clock-like) fashion, looking for a page that has not been accessed recently (i.e., its reference bit has not been set). In doing the sweep, the OS also clears the bits as it examines them, and hence in the worst case will sweep all the way around before replacing a page (in the case that all pages had been accessed).

text: IFFS doesn’t support hard links. Why do you think so (explain)?
answer: In the standard file system, a hard link is represented by having different directory entries (i.e., different path names) point to the same inode; in this way, a user can refer to any of those path name to access the same inode and thus the same data. Thus, inodes serve as a useful single point of indirection mapping file names to data. In IFFS, there is no way for different pathnames to point to the same exact file. Although different directory entries could contain the same pointers to the same data blocks, there is no mechanism to keep the directory entries consistent with each other; if the user appends, truncates, or deletes the file through one name, the other versions will not be updated. Thus, hard links cannot be supported.

text: Explain the “shortest seek time first” (SSTF) disk scheduling algorithm and its primary problem.
